title: Problem 04
markdown:
Show that there are infinitely many $3 \times 3$ matrices $M$ with integer entries such that $M^2 = I$, where $I$ is the $3 \times 3$ identity matrix.

### Solution (adapted from the official solution)
For any integer $k$, define the matrix:

$$M_k = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ k & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.$$

Every entry of $M_k$ is an integer.

Now compute $M_k^2$:

$$M_k^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ k & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ k & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \cdot 1 + 0 + 0 & 0 & 0 \\ k(1) + (-1)(k) + 0 & 0 + (-1)(-1) + 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \cdot 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = I.$$

Since $k$ can be any integer, this gives infinitely many distinct $3 \times 3$ integer matrices satisfying $M^2 = I$.

### Conceptual Explanation
Constructing lower-triangular matrices with diagonal $(1, -1, 1)$ and an arbitrary integer $k$ at position $(2, 1)$ ensures that $(M^2)_{2,1} = k(1) + (-1)k = 0$, while diagonal entries square to 1. This produces an infinite family parameterized by $k \in \mathbb{Z}$.

### Key Technique
Parametric construction of triangular matrix involutions.
